findings.title: FAILED rows at shutdown may read needs_restart=None after clear_all()
Findings converge on how a reader tells a complete lifecycle sequence from a gappy one (D8's reliance on the in-memory drop counter)
findings.why_it_matters: D8 derives the outage length and flap marker from consecutive connection rows, and accepts that a dropped row skews them because "a dropped row is already counted, so a skewed figure is discoverable". The counter lives only in memory, and the ledger's own Assumed section says so (line 234). Four findings attack that same loss-visibility contract from different directions. Finding 5: lifecycle rows share the bounded write queue, so they drop during the very bursts the table is meant to explain, and the evidence of the drop is gone after a restart. Finding 6: for any past session the counter can't make a skew discoverable, though `from_status` already marks a mid-sequence gap and the ledger never tells the reader to use it. Finding 7: retention by `ts` removes the head of a long-running session's sequence, which looks like a gap. Finding 8: the shutdown drain can lose the tail, which looks like a crash. Each proposes its own sentence for #4084 or its own persisted counter. Together they ask whether this ledger should state one completeness contract for the rows (what a reader can trust, and how it sees that a piece is missing) rather than accumulate per-case rules. Re-evaluation is open-ended: it includes whether the ledger should specify any of this or hand it whole to #4084, and whether the cases are limitations to accept and document.
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate the lifecycle rows' completeness contract (D8's reliance on the counter) before addressing Findings 5-8 individually. Open questions: what must a reader be able to detect (mid-sequence drop, head loss, tail loss)? Is the signal in the rows, on the session, or neither? Does this ledger state the contract or hand it to #4084? Which cases are accepted limitations?
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate the lifecycle rows' completeness contract (D8's reliance on the counter) before addressing Findings 5-8 individually. Settled: from_status break rule, head rule, session end from sessions, burst drops accepted, no persisted count

findings.title: The writer call can raise inside the status owners, and the design only promises that drops can't
findings.why_it_matters: The Posture says "no drop affects the lifecycle path that wrote it", but only the three enqueue drop outcomes are specified. The writer also builds a per-kind Pydantic details model, serializes it, and resolves the session, all synchronously inside the owner. A raise there escapes into the owner. In `set_app_status` the registry already holds the new status but the event is never sent, and the exception propagates into start/stop, which is exactly what that method's docstring guards against for the send (`app_lifecycle_instances.py:179-181`). In `set_connection_state`, depending on where the call sits, the transition is either lost or half-applied (`_connection_state` set, but `_connected_event.clear()` and the generation reset skipped, `websocket_service.py:258-267`). In `_handle_recv_task_done` the loop's exception handler swallows it after `fail_all` has already run. `ApiWriteRecorder.enqueue`, the stated precedent, catches only `RuntimeError` (`api_write_recorder.py:203-208`), so copying it doesn't cover a build failure. Also, reaching the writer through `hassette.session_manager` raises `RuntimeError` when services aren't wired (`hassette_accessors.py:94-98`), which a guard inside the writer can't cover. (SE's point about the raising `session_id` property doesn't apply as stated: the writer is a `SessionManager` method, so it checks its own `_session_id`.)
findings.chosen: In the Summary's writer bullet, add: the writer never raises. It wraps session check, details-model build, serialization and enqueue in one `except Exception`, logs with traceback (`exception()`) under the same pacer as the drop WARNING, and counts it under the same new `PipelineCounter` member. The owners reach it by a path that can't raise when services aren't wired (or inside the same guard). In D6, state that the call goes last in `set_connection_state`, after the state assignment and the event/generation bookkeeping; D1 already places the app call between `set_status` and the send. Peer note: this matches OpenTelemetry's error-handling rule that instrumentation must not throw unhandled exceptions at run time (opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/error-handling, not in the brief) and the in-repo `set_app_status` send guard.

findings.title: The read-side order key is unspecified, and `ts` can't serve as one
findings.why_it_matters: D3's block closure and D8's outage and flap derivation depend on consecutive rows. The schema indexes `(ts)` and `(app_key, ts)`, so #4084 will naturally `ORDER BY ts`. `ts` is wall-clock time the writer stamps. Two rows a few awaits apart (DISCONNECTED from the done-callback, then CONNECTING from `handle_connection_failure`) can tie at the clock's resolution, and `LAG()` over a tie is nondeterministic. A wall-clock step reorders rows outright and gives a negative outage. On a Raspberry Pi without an RTC, the clock commonly steps by NTP right after boot, which is when Hassette starts and writes its first rows. The true order already exists: the writer is called synchronously at the change and `enqueue` is a synchronous `put_nowait` onto one FIFO queue with one worker, so `id` order is call order.
findings.chosen: In D5, after the core-columns line, add: `id` is the sequence key (order by `id` within a session, and per instance); `ts` is for display and time-window filtering only, since rows enter one FIFO queue at the moment of change while wall-clock time can tie or step. D8's derivation then cites D5 for the order. Add to D5's Peer divergence line: HA's history and Prefect's state reads order by timestamp (`last_updated_ts`, `timestamp`; from source knowledge, not the brief); Hassette orders by `id` because its single synchronous enqueue makes `id` the exact order and survives a clock step. Leave index choice to #4084.

findings.title: The drop path and WARNING call every `False` from `enqueue` "queue full", but some are a yield to a waiting `submit()`
findings.why_it_matters: `enqueue` returns `False` for a full queue and also when any `submit()` caller is waiting for capacity, which it already counts under `DB_WRITE_QUEUE_YIELDED_TO_SUBMIT` (`database_write_queue.py:274-282`). The ledger's "queue full (`enqueue` returned False)" and a copied `warn_drop` message ("Database write queue is full", `api_write_recorder.py:222`) misname the second cause, and the same dropped row appears under two counters with no note saying so. A reader of #4084's loss count would read every drop as backpressure.
findings.chosen: In the Summary's writer bullet, replace "queue full (`enqueue` returned False)" with "not queued (`enqueue` returned False: a full queue, or yielding to a waiting `submit()`, which `enqueue` also counts under `DB_WRITE_QUEUE_YIELDED_TO_SUBMIT`)", and say the WARNING uses neutral wording ("could not queue lifecycle row"). If the pacer is shared with `ApiWriteRecorder`, the message must be per caller.

findings.title: Lifecycle rows share the bounded write queue, so they drop during the bursts they're meant to explain
findings.why_it_matters: The writer enqueues onto `DatabaseService`'s one queue (`write_queue_max`, default 2000), which also carries persisted log records (`database_write_queue.py:305`), API writes, blocking events, and execution batches and startup registrations through `submit()` (`execution_pipeline.py:313`, `command_executor.py:590-700`). A startup with many apps registering listeners, or an error storm during a reconnect, can fill it or set a waiting `submit()`, and then every lifecycle row in that window is dropped. That window is the "what happened at 05:00" the table exists for. The Posture accepts drops as best-effort, but never says they correlate with incidents.
findings.recommended: A: Accept it. Add to the Posture's failure-handling line that lifecycle rows share the write queue, so drops cluster around the bursts the table records.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: D8's "a dropped row is discoverable" is false for past sessions, and the detector already stored (`from_status`) is never named
findings.why_it_matters: D8's ratified acceptance rests on the drop being counted and so discoverable. The counter is an in-memory `PipelineCounter`; `_finalize_session` persists only the command executor's drop counters (`core.py:655-676`), and the Assumed section says lifecycle counters live only in memory (line 234). So for any session but the live one, #4084 can't tell a clean sequence from a gappy one by the counter. The rows already carry a detector: `from_status` is the owner's real previous state (D5), so a row whose `from_status` differs from the preceding row's `to_status` marks a gap. Two cautions: on app rows `set_status` reports NOT_STARTED as previous after STOPPED removed the entry (`app_registry.py:117, 158`), which isn't a gap; and a dropped final row can't be seen by a chain check.
findings.recommended: A: Rewrite D8's dropped-row reasoning: derived figures are valid only over a sequence with no `from_status` break, #4084 flags a break rather than reporting a number, and an app row with previous NOT_STARTED after STOPPED is continuous. Remove "discoverable via the counter".
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: Retention by `ts` removes the head of a long-running session's sequence
findings.why_it_matters: The new target deletes rows by `ts < cutoff`. The session delete guard keeps the live session (`database_retention.py:386-395`), but not its old child rows. A session that outlives `retention_days` (30 by default) loses its oldest lifecycle rows while still running. D8's anchor "or the session start, if the session never connected" and the from/to chain both reach back to the head. After truncation, the first surviving row's `from_status` has no predecessor, which looks like a drop (Finding 6), and a figure anchored to the session start is computed from rows that are gone.
findings.recommended: A: Say in D8 that a session's first retained row is never a break and never an anchor, and that a derived outage with no preceding row is reported as "since at least <first retained ts>".
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: A lost shutdown tail is indistinguishable from a crash unless the reader is told otherwise
findings.why_it_matters: The final STOPPED and DISCONNECTED rows are the ones a slow drain abandons (Assumed, line 233), and nothing about that loss is persisted beyond a log line (line 234). Those rows are what distinguishes a clean end from a crash in the lifecycle table. The session record does carry it: `stopped_at` and the final status are written by `_finalize_session`. The ledger never tells #4084 to read the end from `sessions` rather than from the last lifecycle row.
findings.chosen: Add one sentence to the Assumed bullet on the bounded drain (line 233): how a session ended comes from `sessions` (`stopped_at`, status), not from its last lifecycle row, so a finalized session whose tail rows are missing ended cleanly with a lost tail.

findings.title: D3's `removed` status is also written for an app disabled in config while blocked
findings.why_it_matters: D3 writes `removed` for an app that "left the blocked set because it left `enabled_manifests`". `enabled_manifests` excludes disabled manifests (`app_registry.py:589-592`), and the caller's own comment says "An app disabled in config since it was blocked comes back unblocked too" (`app_lifecycle_config.py:121-122`). So disabling a blocked app writes `removed`, though its manifest is still configured. The code can tell the two apart (`registry.manifests` still holds disabled ones). The senior engineer's other D3 concern, re-emitting `blocked` on a second reconcile, is already ruled out by D3's "a `blocked` row per newly blocked app"; a build test for it is cheap.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a `removed` row also covers an app disabled in config while blocked; D3 defines `removed` as "left the enabled config".
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a `removed` row also covers an app disabled in config while blocked; D3 defines `removed` as "left the enabled config".
